summary: Calcium gluconate injection (10% = 100 mg/mL; a 10 mL ampoule of 1 g provides ~93 mg / 4.65 mEq / ~2.32 mmol elemental calcium) is used to treat acute symptomatic hypocalcemia and as an antidote for hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity, magnesium sulfate toxicity, calcium channel blocker overdose, and hydrofluoric acid exposure. The usual adult dose is ~1-3 g IV given slowly. It is preferred over calcium chloride peripherally because it is less irritating on extravasation. Rapid IV injection can cause hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest; calcium potentiates digitalis toxicity.
indications: Cardiac membrane stabilization in hyperkalemia (protects the heart; does not lower serum potassium)
Hydrofluoric acid burns / exposure (topical, infiltration, or systemic)
Calcium supplementation when oral intake is inadequate (oral salt also available)

dosage.d: 1-3 g IV; e.g. 1 g (10 mL of 10%) over ~5-10 min, may repeat
dosage.t: Slow IV bolus, then infusion if needed
dosage.n: Follow with continuous infusion for persistent hypocalcemia

dosage.n: Stabilizes myocardium; does not lower potassium - add insulin/dextrose, etc.

dosage.n: For respiratory depression / hyporeflexia from hypermagnesemia

dosage.n: Titrate to blood pressure and perfusion; high doses may be needed

dosage.n: Specialist / poison-center guidance; binds fluoride ion
Cardiac monitoring; avoid scalp/small peripheral veins

admin: Administer SLOWLY by IV - rapid injection causes vasodilation, hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest
Use ECG monitoring during IV administration, especially in patients on digoxin
Preferred over calcium chloride peripherally (less irritating, lower necrosis risk on extravasation), but extravasation can still cause tissue necrosis and calcinosis
Do NOT mix or co-infuse with bicarbonate or phosphate-containing solutions - calcium precipitates
Warm to body temperature and ensure the IV line is patent before giving
Stop the infusion immediately if extravasation is suspected
moa: Calcium is the essential cation for nerve and muscle function, cardiac contractility, and blood coagulation. Administered calcium gluconate dissociates to raise the extracellular ionized calcium concentration, correcting hypocalcemia. In hyperkalemia it raises the cardiac cell membrane threshold potential, restoring the normal gradient between threshold and resting potentials and stabilizing the myocardium against arrhythmia without changing the serum potassium level.

relative: Concomitant digoxin / digitalis therapy (calcium potentiates toxicity - risk of fatal arrhythmia)
Risk of calcium-containing renal calculi or history of nephrolithiasis
Sarcoidosis and other conditions predisposing to hypercalcemia
monitor: ECG during and after IV administration
Serum calcium (ideally ionized) and the calcium x phosphate product
IV site for extravasation, infiltration or tissue necrosis

preg: Calcium crosses the placenta and is required in pregnancy. Use to correct symptomatic maternal hypocalcemia or as an antidote (e.g. magnesium toxicity) when clearly needed; avoid inducing maternal hypercalcemia.
lact: Calcium is a normal constituent of breast milk and IV calcium gluconate is considered compatible with breastfeeding. Maternal supplementation is not expected to harm the breastfed infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment because of the risk of hypercalcemia, soft-tissue/vascular calcification (raised calcium x phosphate product) and calcium-containing renal calculi. Monitor serum calcium closely.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

major: Digoxin / digitalis glycosides - calcium potentiates cardiac toxicity and can precipitate fatal arrhythmias; avoid or give very cautiously with ECG monitoring
IV ceftriaxone (especially in neonates) - precipitation of ceftriaxone-calcium; do not co-administer
moderate: Thiazide diuretics - reduced calcium excretion may cause hypercalcemia
Calcium channel blockers - calcium antagonizes their effect (basis of antidote use)
Vitamin D analogues - increased calcium absorption and hypercalcemia risk
minor: Oral tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, bisphosphonates, levothyroxine - calcium reduces absorption (separate dosing; relevant to oral salt)
Iron salts - reduced iron absorption when taken together orally
interactions.food: Not applicable to the IV product; oral calcium salts may reduce absorption of certain drugs and minerals.
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to acute IV antidote/replacement use.
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum calcium; do not physically mix with bicarbonate or phosphate (precipitation). May affect calcium-dependent lab assays.

common: Sensation of warmth, flushing or tingling during injection
serious: Bradycardia and cardiac arrhythmia with rapid injection
Tissue necrosis and calcinosis from extravasation
rare: Soft-tissue / vascular calcification with chronic excess
Precipitation reactions when mixed with incompatible solutions
emergency: Cardiac arrest from rapid IV injection
Severe arrhythmia, particularly in digitalized patients

monitoring: Serum (ideally ionized) calcium before, during and after correction
Continuous ECG during IV administration, especially with digoxin or hyperkalemia
IV insertion site for extravasation or infiltration
Serum magnesium, phosphate and the calcium x phosphate product
Blood pressure and heart rate during infusion
counsel: This medicine is given into a vein by a clinician and injected slowly
Tell staff right away of pain, burning or swelling at the drip site
Report flushing, palpitations, feeling faint or an irregular heartbeat
Inform the team if you take digoxin or other heart medicines
For oral calcium supplements, separate from certain antibiotics, thyroid and iron tablets
pk: Not classically defined; calcium is regulated homeostatically
Short (~30 min-2 h after a bolus); repeat or infuse for sustained effect
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); do not freeze; discard if precipitate present
pearls: 10% calcium gluconate = 100 mg/mL; a 10 mL (1 g) ampoule provides ~93 mg / 4.65 mEq / ~2.32 mmol elemental calcium
In hyperkalemia calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does NOT lower potassium - still give insulin/dextrose and other measures
Preferred over calcium chloride for peripheral lines (less irritating, lower extravasation-necrosis risk)
Never mix with bicarbonate or phosphate - precipitation
Avoid or use extreme caution with concomitant digoxin - calcium can trigger fatal arrhythmias
missed: Given by a clinician in acute/emergency settings, so a missed dose is not applicable. For an oral calcium gluconate supplement, take the missed dose when remembered; skip it if the next dose is near and do not double up.
overdose: Overdose causes hypercalcemia: nausea, vomiting, constipation, weakness, confusion, polyuria, arrhythmia and, severely, coma. Stop calcium, give IV isotonic saline to promote diuresis, and treat with measures to lower calcium (e.g. loop diuretic with adequate hydration, calcitonin, bisphosphonate; dialysis in severe renal failure). Monitor ECG and serum calcium.
